lead: Some messages surprise you more than others. A symbol that appears rarely carries more information than one that appears all the time. Information theory turns this everyday idea into a number. Self-information measures one symbol; entropy measures the average symbol of a source; information rate converts that average into bits per second. These numbers tell you how much a source can be compressed and how much channel capacity it needs. They sit under PCM bit rates, Huffman coding, and the Shannon capacity formula used to plan a microwave or fibre link.
prereq: You need: probability, random variables and the idea of a random source (see the probability and random variables review).

blocks.text: A discrete source emits one symbol at a time from a finite alphabet of M symbols. Call symbol i's probability p<sub>i</sub>, with 0 < p<sub>i</sub> ≤ 1 and Σp<sub>i</sub> = 1. The self-information of symbol i is the surprise when that symbol arrives. A rare symbol has small p<sub>i</sub>, so it carries a large amount of information. A certain symbol, p<sub>i</sub> = 1, carries zero information because you already knew it was coming.

blocks.where: I(x<sub>i</sub>) is the self-information of symbol i in bits; p<sub>i</sub> is its probability; log₂ is the logarithm to base 2.

blocks.text: The logarithm is there because independent symbols must add their information. If two independent symbols have probabilities p<sub>i</sub> and p<sub>j</sub>, their joint probability is p<sub>i</sub>p<sub>j</sub>. We want total information to be the sum: I(p<sub>i</sub>p<sub>j</sub>) = I(p<sub>i</sub>) + I(p<sub>j</sub>). Only a logarithm turns a product into a sum: log(1/(p<sub>i</sub>p<sub>j</sub>)) = log(1/p<sub>i</sub>) + log(1/p<sub>j</sub>). Base 2 makes the unit the bit, the information in one fair coin toss.

Base e gives the nat and base 10 gives the hartley. Conversions: 1 nat = log₂ e ≈ 1.4427 bits; 1 hartley = log₂ 10 ≈ 3.3219 bits. In communication problems, write bits unless the question names another unit.
H(X) = Σ pᵢ log₂(1/pᵢ) = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ  bits/symbol
blocks.where: H(X) is the source entropy in bits per symbol; the sums run over the M symbols, i = 1 to M; p<sub>i</sub> is the probability of symbol i; a term with p<sub>i</sub> = 0 is taken as 0.

blocks.text: Entropy is the average self-information per symbol. Before a symbol arrives it is the uncertainty about which symbol will come. After the symbol arrives it is the average information you gained. A source whose symbols have nearly equal probabilities has high entropy; a source that almost always sends the same symbol has low entropy. Some syllabi call H the average information or the uncertainty of the source.

For fixed M, H is largest when all M symbols are equally likely: Hmax = log₂ M. A 4-level equal source has H = 2 bits/symbol; an 8-level equal source has H = 3 bits/symbol. Unequal probabilities always give less than log₂ M. The binary case uses p for one symbol and 1−p for the other: H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1−p) log₂(1−p). It peaks at 1 bit when p = 0.5 and falls to 0 at p = 0 or p = 1. Entropy is the lower bound that Huffman coding tries to reach.

blocks.where: R is the information rate in bits per second; r<sub>s</sub> is the symbol rate in symbols per second; H is the entropy in bits per symbol.

blocks.text: The symbol rate says how fast symbols arrive. The information rate says how fast information arrives. A source emitting 4 symbols with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8 has H = 1.75 bits/symbol. At r<sub>s</sub> = 2000 symbols/s, R = 2000 × 1.75 = 3500 bit/s. If the 4 symbols were equally likely, H would be 2 bits/symbol and R would be 4000 bit/s at the same symbol rate.

items: An 8-level equal source has H = log₂ 8 = 3 bits/symbol. At 1000 symbols/s, R = 3000 bit/s.
Bits per symbol is an entropy answer. Bits per second is an information-rate answer. Multiply by r<sub>s</sub> and keep the units.
These formulas assume a memoryless source: each symbol's probability does not depend on earlier symbols. Dependence between symbols is handled by conditional entropy (see mutual information).

blocks.text: Information rate is the number you compare with channel capacity. If R is below capacity, reliable transmission is possible; if R is above capacity, it is not. That comparison is the whole point of measuring a source before designing the link.

examples.question: A memoryless source emits four symbols with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/8 at a symbol rate of 2000 symbols per second. Find the information carried by each symbol, the source entropy, and the information rate.
steps: List the probabilities: p<sub>1</sub> = 1/2, p<sub>2</sub> = 1/4, p<sub>3</sub> = 1/8, p<sub>4</sub> = 1/8. The symbol rate is r<sub>s</sub> = 2000 symbols/s.
examples.answer: The four symbols carry 1 bit, 2 bits, 3 bits and 3 bits; the entropy is 1.75 bits/symbol; the information rate is 3500 bit/s.
examples.check:
import math
p = [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125]
rs = 2000
inf = [-math.log2(pi) for pi in p]
for value in inf:
    print(value)
H = sum(pi * ii for pi, ii in zip(p, inf))
print(H)
print(rs * H)

examples.question: A voice signal band-limited to 4 kHz is sampled at the Nyquist rate. Each sample is quantised to one of four levels whose probabilities are 1/8, 3/8, 3/8 and 1/8, and successive samples are independent. Find the entropy per sample and the information rate. How much higher would the rate be with four equally likely levels?
steps: Nyquist rate: r<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 4000 = 8000 samples/s. Each sample is one source symbol.
Self-information: the two outer levels carry log₂ 8 = 3 bits each; the two inner levels carry log₂(8/3) = 1.415 bits each.
Information rate: R = r<sub>s</sub>H = 8000 × 1.811 = 14 490 bit/s ≈ 14.5 kbit/s.
Equal levels: H<sub>max</sub> = log₂ 4 = 2 bits/sample and R = 8000 × 2 = 16 000 bit/s, which is 1510 bit/s (10.4 %) more.
examples.answer: H = 1.811 bits/sample and R ≈ 14.5 kbit/s; equally likely levels would give 16 kbit/s.

traps: Using log₁₀ or ln and still writing the answer in bits. A base-10 answer is in hartleys and a base-e answer is in nats; convert to bits or change the base.
Quoting bits per symbol when the question asks for bits per second. Multiply by the symbol rate and check the units.
Assuming every M-level source has entropy log₂ M. That maximum holds only when all M symbols are equally likely.
Forgetting that p log₂ p tends to 0 as p tends to 0, so a zero-probability symbol adds no term to the entropy.
Confusing the self-information of one symbol with the average entropy of the whole source.

quiz.q: Define the self-information of a symbol with probability p and state its unit when the logarithm is base 2.
quiz.a: I = log₂(1/p) = −log₂ p. The unit is the bit.

quiz.q: Why does using a logarithm make information from independent symbols add?
quiz.a: Independent probabilities multiply: p<sub>ij</sub> = p<sub>i</sub>p<sub>j</sub>. The logarithm turns this product into a sum: log(1/(p<sub>i</sub>p<sub>j</sub>)) = log(1/p<sub>i</sub>) + log(1/p<sub>j</sub>).

quiz.q: An 8-level source has equal symbol probabilities and emits 5000 symbols per second. Find the entropy and the information rate.
quiz.a: For equal probabilities, H = log₂ 8 = 3 bits/symbol. R = r<sub>s</sub>H = 5000 × 3 = 15000 bit/s.

quiz.q: A binary source has p(0) = 0.9 and p(1) = 0.1. Find its entropy.
Can the entropy of an M-level source exceed log₂ M? Explain.
quiz.a: No. H is maximised when all M symbols are equally likely, giving H = log₂ M. Any unequal distribution makes some symbols more predictable and lowers the average surprise.

quiz.q: Two 4-level sources have the same symbol rate but different probability distributions. Which one has the larger information rate, and why?
quiz.a: The source with the flatter distribution has the larger entropy and hence the larger R = r<sub>s</sub>H. A distribution closer to equal probabilities carries more average information per symbol.

quiz.q: Name the information units for logarithm base e and base 10.
quiz.a: Base e gives the nat; base 10 gives the hartley.

beyond: Not for the exam. Entropy is the first bridge from communication to machine learning: decision trees split on information gain, and language models report cross-entropy or perplexity. The same formula estimates password strength and appears in lossless compression tools. Search next for Shannon's source coding theorem, relative entropy (KL divergence), and rate-distortion theory. These ideas extend the fixed bit count of pulse code modulation to variable-length compression.
